newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain prisoner mystery divides parties.
newsitem.headline: Spain prisoner mystery divides parties.

text.p: Serious injuries suffered by a captured ETA assassination suspect drove a new wedge between Spain's ruling party and its Basque nationalist allies on Friday.

"I have too many questions and few answers," said Basque regional government President Jose Antonio Ardanza about Fernando Elejalde, who was arrested on Tuesday at a murder scene and taken to hospital two days later with fractured vertebrae and a ruptured kidney.
Ardanza's Basque Nationalist Party (PNV), the leading political force in the region and an ally of the central government's ruling Popular Party, alleged the prisoner had been tortured.

The government, which scored a rare coup with the capture of an ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) guerrilla on the scene of the crime, said Elejalde probably sustained the injuries in a chase and gun-battle with police just after the fatal shooting of a prison psychologist on the doorstep of his home in the northern city of San Sebastian.

The PNV's distrust of the government's version underscores its growing uneasiness over the treatment of Basque prisoners and of Interior Minister Jaime Mayor Oreja's conduct of the battle against separatist rebels.
PNV support in parliament is a cushion that gives conservative Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar a comfortable majority, but is not essential for his government's survival.
In a show of discontent, the PNV voted with the opposition on a few legislative proposals this week and Ardanza stayed away from an important debate between Aznar and all regional heads.
On Tuesday a PNV official assailed Mayor Oreja in parliament for hushing up the fact that an ETA prisoner who committed suicide last month had his hands and feet bound when found dead.

Anxious to avoid a repeat of that scene, the Interior Ministry made public plenty of details on Elejalde's condition on Thursday night and swiftly announced it was opening an investigation which would be concluded 72 hours later.
The PP and PNV have been sparring for months over how to end a 29-year conflict with ETA, but this week, clashes intensified.

"In the matter of pacification, PNV and PP are diametrically opposed to one another," Carlos Iturgaiz, the PP's leader in the Basque region, said on Friday. "While the PNV wants to negotiate no matter what with ETA, in the PP we say clearly we are not negotiating with a band of assassins."
The PNV has urged the government to negotiate peace but they have firmly refused to talk unless ETA renounces violence first.

Another source of acrimony is the government's prisoner policy. The PNV wants Basque prisoners, including more than 500 ETA inmates, now dispersed throughout the country moved to jails in or near the Basque region.
The government rejects a blanket transfer and says it will only consider transfers case-by-case basis.
Mayor Oreja has come in for particularly harsh criticism by PNV officials who say he does not understand the prisoner issue.
They were angered when he refused to meet a Basque parliament delegation pressing for a prisoner transfer.
"In this divergence... the PNV feels uncomfortable and is aiming all its missiles at the Interior Minister," Iturgaiz said.
Gestoras Amnestias, a prisoner advocacy group sympathetic to ETA, says 11 ETA prisoners have died in jail since 1978, most of them for lack of proper medical treatment.
